name: PhotoPills
tagline: Mobile planner for photographers: sun, moon and Milky Way positions on a map, plus exposure and depth of field calculators.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold as a one-time mobile app purchase rather than a subscription, which changes the math on building your own.

verdictSummary: Every number PhotoPills shows you is computable from open astronomy libraries and a public map tile layer. An agent can give you a pin on a map, sun and moon rise/set azimuth lines, golden and blue hour windows, galactic center altitude, and the usual depth of field and 500-rule calculators in one session, and it will be correct to within a rounding error. What it cannot give you in one session is the part people actually open the app for in the field: the augmented reality viewfinder that paints the Milky Way arc over the real horizon through your phone camera, working offline, on a cliff, at 3am. Browser sensor APIs for compass heading are flaky and permission-gated, and terrain obstruction modeling needs an elevation dataset you have to go get. So: the desk-planning half is a one-shot, the on-location half is not.
coreLoopDIY: Drop a pin on a map, pick a date and time, and see sun, moon and galactic center azimuth lines drawn from that pin plus the relevant twilight windows and camera calculators.
requirements: A browser, no server needed beyond a static host
Public map tiles (OpenStreetMap) and an open astronomy library
Your own phone for anything you want to do in the field, with no offline guarantee
whatYouLose: The AR viewfinder, which is the feature that justifies the purchase for most owners
Reliable offline use on a mobile device with no signal
Terrain and horizon obstruction, so your web version will happily tell you the sun rises behind a mountain
Eclipse, meteor shower and supermoon tables, plus the curated how-to content bundled around the tool
Years of edge-case correctness in timezones, DST and high-latitude twilight that someone else already debugged
moatNotes: The moat is a phone's camera, compass and accelerometer fused into something trustworthy enough to frame a shot with. That is a native app problem, not a math problem.
whyPeopleStillPay: It is a one-time purchase for a tool you use standing in a field with cold hands, which is a very different reliability bar than a tab you have open at your desk. The astronomy is free; the confidence that the arc on your screen is actually where the Milky Way will be, aligned to the ridge in front of you, is what you bought. Also, at one-time mobile app pricing, the break-even against your own time is roughly twenty minutes.
notes: Build the planner, keep the app for the field. They are not actually competing for the same moment.
prompt:
Build a local-first web app called "Shot Planner" for planning outdoor photography around the sun, moon and Milky Way.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles for the map
- the astronomy-engine npm package for all celestial math
- plain CSS, no UI framework
- localStorage for saved locations, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry

Core behavior:
1. Full-screen map. Click to drop a single pin. Show lat/lon and elevation-free coordinates in a panel.
2. Date and time controls: date picker, a time slider across the selected day, and a "now" button. Resolve the timezone from the pin coordinates using the tz-lookup package and display all times in that local timezone, with the offset shown explicitly.
3. From the pin, draw directional lines on the map for: sunrise azimuth, sunset azimuth, current sun azimuth, moonrise azimuth, moonset azimuth, current moon azimuth, and current galactic center azimuth. Use distinct colors, label each, and make them toggleable. Dash the lines for bodies that are currently below the horizon.
4. Info panel for the selected date: sunrise, sunset, solar noon, civil/nautical/astronomical twilight start and end, blue hour and golden hour windows, moonrise, moonset, moon illumination percent, moon phase name, and the window when the galactic center is above 10 degrees altitude with the sun below -18 degrees.
5. Calculators tab: depth of field and hyperfocal distance (sensor presets for full frame, APS-C, micro four thirds, plus custom circle of confusion), field of view from focal length, the 500 rule and NPF rule for star trails, and a timelapse calculator (interval, duration, clip length, frame count).
6. Save and reload named locations from localStorage. Export and import the whole set as JSON.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt:
- augmented reality or camera overlay
- device compass or orientation sensors
- terrain or horizon obstruction modeling
- eclipse paths, meteor showers, any third-party weather or elevation API

Quality bar: handle high-latitude days with no sunrise or sunset without crashing, handle DST transitions, and verify sun azimuth output against a known reference for one test location in a unit test. Write a README explaining the math sources and stating plainly that the app is for desk planning, not field use.

Run locally with npm run dev. No secrets needed; if you add any config later, put it in .env.
